newsitem.title: USA: Christian Coalition names new leadership team.
newsitem.headline: Christian Coalition names new leadership team.

text.p: The Christian Coalition, a powerful conservative grassroots force in American politics, Wednesday introduced a new dual leadership team to replace its charismatic director Ralph Reed.

The organisation's founder, television evangelist Pat Robertson, named former Reagan administration Cabinet member Don Hodel as president and chief executive officer and former Republican lawmaker Randy Tate as executive director.
"God has shown his faithfulness in the form of a double blessing. For Ralph's replacement we have two outstanding leaders of enormous talent," Robertson told a news conference on Capitol Hill.

Under Reed's leadership over the past eight years, the Christian Coalition grew from nothing into a movement with almost 2 million members and an annual budget of some $30 million. It is now acknowledged to be perhaps the most influential single faction in Republican Party politics.

The organisation distributed some 45 million voter guides just before last November's elections through a network of 125,000 churches. In many congressional districts it has become virtually impossible to get elected without the support of its members.

But Robertson, who will become chairman of the organisation's board of directors, said he had even more ambitious goals in mind for the next four years -- to double the number of candidates the coalition trained for public office and to double its number of legislative initiatives.

Hodel, 62, served as energy secretary under President Ronald Reagan from 1982-85 and interior secretary from 1985-89. He has been in private life pursuing various business interests over the past eight years.
"I am here today because I believe that the moral and cultural problems we face as a nation are as real a threat to the promise of America as any we have faced," he said.
He listed his goals as advancing school choice, safe streets, opposing abortion, supporting a balanced budget and reaching out to blacks, Hispanics, Catholics and Jews.
Tate, 31, was elected to Congress from the state of Washington in 1994 but lost his seat last November.

"Clearly I could have chosen to again pursue public office. After much prayer and reflection I concluded that this position affords an even greater opportunity to shape the future of America," he said.
Robertson made it clear Hodel would be the senior partner in the new leadership. Both men take up their posts next week.
Reed is leaving to set up a political consultancy that will focus on training grassroots conservative activists for political office.
